vignette:
He is 31, a South Eastern Asian man, married, and works as a judge in a busy provincial court. On the bench he is known for being measured, careful with language, and difficult to rattle. He tells his story in that same controlled way at first, as if he is drafting findings for a case. But as the sessions go on, the orderliness of his account gives way to the felt experience beneath it.

The disaster happens just before dawn, during the rainy season, when he and his wife are asleep in their second-floor apartment. He wakes to a low, unnatural sound—part roar, part grinding—and then to the bed moving beneath him. For a second he thinks he is still dreaming. Then the wardrobe doors slam open, the ceiling fan swings violently, and the power cuts out. His wife is shouting his name. He remembers the dark more than anything: the dark, the shaking, and the noise of concrete cracking somewhere nearby.

He pulls his wife off the bed and toward the doorway, remembering some half-forgotten advice about standing in a frame. But the building is lurching so hard they cannot stay upright. He says the floor feels “alive,” as if it is trying to throw them down. They crouch together, arms over their heads, while glass shatters in the kitchen and car alarms begin screaming outside. He is certain, in those seconds, that the building is going to collapse with them inside it. He thinks with terrible clarity, This is how we die.

When the shaking stops, they run barefoot down the stairwell with the neighbors, stepping over broken plaster and spilled water. Outside, the street is chaos. People are crying, calling for family members, staring upward. A building across the road has partially caved in. Dust hangs in the air like smoke. There are aftershocks, sharp and sudden, each one sending the crowd into another wave of panic. He and his wife spend the rest of the morning in an open parking area, afraid to go back indoors. His phone does not work. He cannot reach his parents for hours. He watches rescue workers pull debris away from a collapsed storefront and still remembers the sound a woman makes when she recognizes the shoe of someone trapped underneath.

In the weeks after, he tells himself he is lucky. His wife is alive. Their apartment is damaged but standing. He returns to work quickly, partly from duty and partly because routine feels safer than idleness. In court, he puts on his robe, reviews affidavits, and speaks in the steady voice people expect from him. But his body does not seem to accept that the danger is over. When a truck passes the courthouse and the floor gives the slightest vibration, his chest tightens before he can think. He glances at the ceiling, the walls, the exit. If someone drops a stack of files behind him, he startles so hard his hands shake.

At home, sleep becomes difficult. He lies beside his wife listening for movement in the building—the elevator cables, plumbing in the walls, wind against the windows—and every small sound seems like a warning. When he does fall asleep, he wakes drenched in sweat, back in the dark apartment, hearing concrete split open. Some nights he grips his wife’s arm to make sure she is there. She tells him gently that he is crushing her hand, and he lets go, ashamed.

He avoids enclosed spaces whenever he can. He begins taking the stairs only if he has to, but he hates stairwells too, the boxed-in feeling of them, the memory of fleeing down in darkness. He starts arriving early to court so he can choose a seat near a door in chambers. During hearings he notices himself tracking where everyone would run in an emergency rather than listening fully to testimony. This troubles him deeply. He has built his identity around concentration, fairness, and self-command. Now he loses fragments of proceedings and asks clerks to repeat details he knows he should have heard.

His wife wants to visit her sister in a high-rise in the capital, and he makes excuses for months. He tells her he is too busy, that the travel is inconvenient. Eventually she asks, not angrily, “Are you afraid to go up?” He says no too quickly. He sees the hurt on her face because by then his world has narrowed around what feels safe. He prefers open spaces, low buildings, routes he has already checked in his mind. During family gatherings he sits near gates or courtyards. When relatives talk about rebuilding, about how everyone must move on, he goes quiet.

He is not numb so much as divided. Part of him knows the earthquake is over. Another part remains poised inside it, scanning, bracing, calculating. He becomes more irritable with colleagues, especially when they are careless or late, as if preparedness itself could ward off catastrophe. He keeps an emergency bag in his car, then another in his chambers, then one by the apartment door. He checks them repeatedly: water, flashlight, documents, charger. He knows the repetition is excessive, but checking briefly relieves the pressure in his chest.

What disturbs him most is the loss of trust in the ordinary world. Floors, walls, sleep, morning rain—none of them feel neutral anymore. He says that before the disaster he believed solid things were solid. Now every room carries a question. Even on calm days, while delivering judgment in a quiet courtroom, he sometimes feels the ghost of motion under his feet and has to pause, just for a second, to tell himself that the building is still.
